topic: EPA general permit: who is covered
rule: 40 CFR 229.1(a) grants a general permit (no application) to (1) anyone subject to MPRSA Title I to transport human remains from the United States for burial at sea, and (2) owners/operators of US-registered or US-flagged vessels or aircraft, and US government entities, to transport human remains from any location and bury them at sea.
quote: are hereby granted a general permit to transport human remains from any location for the purpose of burial at sea
appliesTo: Any vessel departing a US port carrying remains; any US-flagged vessel anywhere
notes: Text retrieved from the eCFR versioner API (www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-01/title-40.xml?part=229&section=229.1). Most large cruise ships are foreign-flagged, so the 'from any location' branch does not reach them; the 'from the United States' branch does when the ship departed a US port with the remains aboard.

rule: Cremated remains may be placed in or on ocean waters at any depth, but no closer than 3 nautical miles from land. 'Land' is measured from the territorial-sea baseline closest to the site (40 CFR 229.1(b)).
quote: Cremated remains shall be buried in or on ocean waters without regard to the depth limitations specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section provided that such burial shall take place no closer than 3 nautical miles from land.
appliesTo: Burials under the EPA general permit
notes: The 600-foot depth rule in (a)(2) applies only to non-cremated (whole-body) burials. Because 'land' is the baseline, 3 nm is counted from the baseline, not from the visible beach, which can matter in bays.

rule: Flowers and wreaths may be placed at the burial site under the general permit only if made of materials readily decomposable in the marine environment.
quote: Flowers and wreaths consisting of materials which are readily decomposable in the marine environment may be disposed of
appliesTo: Burials under the EPA general permit
notes: The regulation text itself does not list banned items (plastic, metal, balloons). Statements that non-decomposable items need a separate permit come from EPA web guidance, which could not be opened (see US-06).

rule: Every burial under the general permit must be reported within 30 days to the EPA Regional Administrator of the Region from which the vessel carrying the remains departed.
quote: All burials conducted under this general permit shall be reported within 30 days to the Regional Administrator of the Region from which the vessel carrying the remains departed.
appliesTo: The person conducting the burial (in practice the family or the vessel operator)
notes: The regulation does not say who files; EPA guidance reportedly expects the person conducting the burial or the vessel operator. Not verified.

rule: EPA operates an online Burial at Sea Reporting Tool for the 30-day report, reportedly at https://burialatsea.epa.gov/; it asks for the deceased's name, burial date, departure location, type of remains, operator contact and coordinates where known.

Its statements on non-decomposable items, inland waters and aircraft could not be read.

topic: MPRSA scope: what 'ocean waters' and 'dumping' mean
rule: EPA's ocean dumping regulations prohibit, without a permit: transporting any material from the United States to dump it in ocean waters; for US-registered or US-flagged vessels, transporting material from any location to dump it; and dumping material transported from outside the US into the US territorial sea or the contiguous zone to 12 nm where it may affect the territorial sea or US territory. 'Ocean waters' are the waters seaward of the baseline, including the territorial sea and contiguous zone.
quote: No person shall dump any material transported from a location outside the United States: (i) Into the territorial sea of the United States
appliesTo: US-flagged vessels anywhere; any vessel transporting material from the US; any vessel dumping in the US territorial sea
notes: Text from the eCFR API. These provisions implement MPRSA section 101 (33 U.S.C. 1411); the statute itself was not opened (uscode.house.gov blocked). Consequence: a foreign-flagged cruise ship that loaded the remains abroad and scatters them on the high seas outside 12 nm is outside MPRSA; the same ship departing Miami with the remains aboard is inside it.

topic: Inland waters and the Clean Water Act
rule: EPA guidance reportedly states that the MPRSA general permit covers only ocean waters, and that scattering in inland waters (rivers, lakes, bays landward of the baseline) may fall under the Clean Water Act and state rules; families are told to check with the state.
citation: Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. 1251 et seq.; EPA Burial at Sea page
appliesTo: Scattering landward of the baseline
notes: Not opened in this session: the research environment's network allowlist blocked this host (DNS failure), and the shared web-search budget was exhausted after four searches. Status is 'couldn't verify', not evidence that the statement is false. Do not state the exact EPA wording until the page is read. The 40 CFR 220.2 'ocean waters' definition (US-07) confirms that waters landward of the baseline are outside the general permit.

topic: Glacier Bay National Park and Preserve
rule: In any NPS area, scattering cremated human ashes is prohibited except under a permit or in designated areas on conditions set by the superintendent. Glacier Bay's waters are park waters, so this rule applies there; no Glacier Bay-specific ash-scattering page was found.
quote: The scattering of human ashes from cremation is prohibited, except pursuant to the terms and conditions of a permit, or in designated areas according to conditions which may be established by the superintendent.
appliesTo: Anyone in a National Park System unit, including cruise passengers in Glacier Bay
notes: The rule text is confirmed via eCFR. Whether 36 CFR 2.62 reaches waters of Glacier Bay depends on NPS jurisdiction over those waters (36 CFR 1.2); Glacier Bay's vessel rules (36 CFR part 13, subpart N) contain no provision on ashes (searched; none found). The park's compendium (home.nps.gov) could not be opened. A web search found no Glacier Bay ash page; it suggested contacting the park (907-697-2230). A cruise line's own policy cannot substitute for an NPS permit.

topic: NPS parks with ash-scattering permit pages
rule: Several NPS units publish special-use-permit pages for scattering cremated remains (e.g. Gulf Islands, Cape Lookout, Biscayne, Yellowstone), showing that the 36 CFR 2.62 permit route is used in practice, including in coastal and marine parks.
appliesTo: Visitors to those parks
notes: URLs found by web search: home.nps.gov/guis/planyourvisit/scattering-remains-permits.htm, home.nps.gov/calo/planyourvisit/sup-cremains.htm, nps.gov/bisc/..., home.nps.gov/yell/planyourvisit/ashscattering.htm. Pages not read in full.

topic: National Marine Sanctuaries: Monterey Bay, cruise ships
rule: In Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, discharging or depositing any material from a cruise ship is prohibited except clean engine/generator cooling water, exhaust, clean bilge water or anchor wash. Cremated remains are not on that exception list.
quote: Discharging or depositing from within or into the Sanctuary any material or other matter from a cruise ship except clean vessel engine cooling water
appliesTo: Cruise ships in Monterey Bay NMS
notes: Text from eCFR API (part 922, 2026-11-01). The prohibitions can be lifted by a sanctuary permit or authorization (see US-15), not by a cruise line's policy. Whether NOAA treats ash scattering as a 'discharge or deposit' in practice is not stated in the regulation; NOAA guidance could not be opened.

topic: National Marine Sanctuaries: Greater Farallones, cruise ships
rule: Greater Farallones NMS uses the same structure: discharges from vessels other than cruise ships have listed exceptions, and cruise-ship discharges are separately restricted. No exception for cremated remains appears.
quote: Discharging or depositing from within or into the Sanctuary, other than from a cruise ship, any material or other matter except
appliesTo: Vessels in Greater Farallones NMS
notes: Text from eCFR API; full cruise-ship subparagraph not quoted here.

rule: Channel Islands NMS prohibits discharging or depositing any material within or into the sanctuary except listed items (fishing bait, certain treated sewage, etc.). Cremated remains are not listed.
quote: Discharging or depositing from within or into the Sanctuary any material or other matter except
appliesTo: Vessels in Channel Islands NMS
notes: Text from eCFR API.

topic: National Marine Sanctuaries: Florida Keys and Hawaiian Humpback
rule: Florida Keys NMS prohibits discharging or depositing any material from within the sanctuary except fishing bait, routine vessel water and cooling water/exhaust. Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale NMS prohibits discharges only where the activity requires a federal or state permit and is conducted without it or out of compliance, so a burial complying with the EPA general permit appears not to breach it. A Florida Keys sanctuary page reportedly says ashes may be scattered only in federal sanctuary waters more than 3 nm from land, with a permit form.
quote: Requires a Federal or State permit, license, lease, or other authorization
appliesTo: Vessels in those sanctuaries
notes: Regulation text confirmed via eCFR; the Hawaii reading is an inference from the text, not an agency statement. Florida Keys guidance (floridakeys.noaa.gov/permits/special-use.html) known only from a search summary; NOAA hosts were blocked.

rule: NOAA may issue special use permits only for activity categories it has noticed in the Federal Register. NOAA's permit materials reportedly list 'disposal of cremated human remains within or into' sanctuaries as a special-use-permit category; a 2013 Federal Register notice proposed dropping a 'commercial operator' limit so private individuals could qualify. Superintendents may also issue ONMS 'authorizations' of another agency's approval in certain sanctuaries.
quote: The Director will not issue a special use permit for any category of activity unless the Director has published a notice in the Federal Register
appliesTo: Operators and individuals scattering in sanctuaries
notes: 922.31/922.36 text confirmed via eCFR. The cremated-remains category and the 2013 proposal are known only from search summaries; the final outcome of the 2013 proposal was not found. sanctuaries.noaa.gov/management/permits/special.html could not be opened.

rule: Under UNCLOS a coastal state's sovereignty extends over a territorial sea of up to 12 nm from the baseline (Arts. 2-3); in a contiguous zone up to 24 nm it may enforce customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary laws (Art. 33). A cruise ship inside a country's territorial sea is subject to that country's laws, including any on scattering ashes.
appliesTo: All ships in a coastal state's waters
notes: Not opened in this session: the research environment's network allowlist blocked this host (DNS failure), and the shared web-search budget was exhausted after four searches. Status is 'couldn't verify', not evidence that the statement is false. The 12 nm and 24 nm limits are standard treaty text, but no quotation was retrieved this session. The US is not a party to UNCLOS but asserts a 12 nm territorial sea and accepts these provisions as customary law (not verified here).

rule: On the high seas a ship is subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of its flag state, save in exceptional cases (UNCLOS Art. 92). A foreign-flagged cruise ship scattering ashes beyond any state's waters is governed mainly by its flag state's law (e.g. Bahamas, Panama, Malta, Bermuda, Italy) and by any law of the state where the remains were loaded.
appliesTo: Ships beyond national jurisdiction
notes: Not opened in this session: the research environment's network allowlist blocked this host (DNS failure), and the shared web-search budget was exhausted after four searches. Status is 'couldn't verify', not evidence that the statement is false. Flag-state laws on scattering ashes (Bahamas, Panama, Malta, Bermuda) were not located.

rule: UNCLOS requires states to regulate dumping; dumping in the territorial sea, EEZ or onto the continental shelf requires the coastal state's express prior approval (Art. 210(5)); enforcement lies with the coastal state, the flag state and the state where the material was loaded (Art. 216).
appliesTo: States; indirectly ship operators
notes: Not opened in this session: the research environment's network allowlist blocked this host (DNS failure), and the shared web-search budget was exhausted after four searches. Status is 'couldn't verify', not evidence that the statement is false. Whether scattering ashes is 'dumping' under UNCLOS depends on the definition and national practice (see INT-04).

rule: The 1972 London Convention and 1996 London Protocol regulate deliberate disposal at sea of wastes or other matter from vessels. No IMO or Protocol decision addressing cremated human remains was found. National practice differs: the US treats burial of human remains, including ashes, as ocean dumping authorized by a general permit (40 CFR 229.1), while other states reportedly exempt ash scattering from licensing.
citation: London Convention 1972 Art. III; London Protocol 1996 Arts. 1, 4 and Annex 1
appliesTo: Contracting states
notes: A web search found no IMO statement on cremated remains (searched IMO leaflet and LC/LP meeting reports via Columbia Law mirrors). 'Not found' is not proof that none exists. The search reported 87 Parties to the Convention (LC 47 report, Oct. 2025) and Protocol entry into force on 24 March 2006; not verified directly. 40 CFR 220.1(b) confirms the US applies London Convention standards through its rules.

topic: MARPOL Annex V and special areas
rule: MARPOL Annex V governs discharge of ship-generated garbage, with stricter rules in special areas (e.g. Mediterranean, Baltic, Wider Caribbean, North Sea, Antarctic). Whether a ceremonial scattering of cremated remains counts as 'garbage' under Annex V was not established; no IMO statement was found.
appliesTo: Ships of MARPOL parties

Status is 'couldn't verify', not evidence that the statement is false. Do not tell readers MARPOL bans or allows ash scattering until the Annex text and IMO guidelines are checked.

rule: Marine protected areas carry their own rules, often stricter than general ocean-disposal law. US examples confirmed above (sanctuaries restrict discharges, including from cruise ships; NPS waters need a permit for ashes). Outside the US, protected-area rules were not checked.

rule: A cruise line's permission is a private policy, not legal authorization.
